summary: Redwood AE/SE walked RiverMark SRE and platform team through the Console's request-level telemetry, log stitching, KV cache visibility and error decomposition workflow. Team agreed to a short pilot benchmark and exchange of security and trace artifacts.
transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-07-01 14:00 UTC | Duration: 55 minutes | Attendees: Sophie, Liam (Redwood), Aisha, Tom, Marta, Kevin (RiverMark)

[00:00] Sophie Martinez: hey everyone thanks for carving out time. we're gonna do a deep-ish walkthrough of the console request telemetry, the request stitching, and how you'd debug errors end-to-end. we have about 50-ish minutes, sound good?
[00:08] Aisha Patel: yep that's great. our big problem is intermittent latency spikes and a couple of misrouted fallbacks we saw last month.
[00:15] Tom Reynolds: and hi, i'm mostly interested in how to map our internal request ids to what appears in the console.
[00:22] Liam Chen: cool, we'll start with the request timeline and then show playback + how we show K V cache state. quick note, i've preloaded a RiverMark sample trace into a sandbox — there may be some redactions, it's synthetic-ish.

[02:05] Liam Chen: ok pulling up the console...so this is the request inspector, you'll see the top bar with overall latency breakdown: tokenization, server compute, external calls, kv-cache. the tricky thing is the prefix cache shows as a percent, but sometimes the viz reads low when we have ongoing partial hits — that's a UI quirk.
[02:40] Marta Kline: when you say prefix cache, do you mean the prompt prefix that's cached between turns?
[02:47] Liam Chen: yeah exactly. the console calls it "prefix/KV" in the breakdown. sometimes auto-generated labels come out weird in the export so you'll see variations.

[04:10] Sophie Martinez: Aisha you mentioned spikes, can you remind us what you saw? was it tail latency or sustained CPU?
[04:18] Aisha Patel: mostly tail. a few requests jumped to 800-900ms token-time while baseline was around 120-150ms. they often coincided with large multi-turn contexts.
[04:28] Liam Chen: that screams cache churn + batch packing variance. if you have many long contexts they push sequence length distribution and kernel selection changes on the runtime.

[06:00] Tom Reynolds: is there a way to filter traces to only show requests where KV cache was a miss?
[06:05] Liam Chen: yep. on the left you can add a filter: request.kv_cache_hit == false. we also surface an event called cache_eviction which helps correlate. note: transcription sometimes writes that as "cache eviction" without underscore in exports.

[07:35] [screen share noise] Liam Chen: here I'm selecting a single request — see the timeline lane? the purple block is model compute, the green is prefix retrieval, red is external webhooks. if you hover you'll get per-stage latencies but if you click play it rewinds and does a replay of the whole request.
[08:12] Aisha Patel: when you replay, does it run the model again or just reconstruct the recorded events?
[08:18] Liam Chen: it's a playback of recorded telemetry — we don't re-run models in the console playback. it's intended to reproduce timing and sequence of events. for active replays you can kick off a local re-run in a dedicated sandbox though.

[09:45] Marta Kline: we have a specific concern: sometimes requests fallback to a smaller model silently and we only notice from degraded outputs later. can the console show model fallbacks?
[09:53] Liam Chen: yes, each request step has an artifact called resolver.decisions — you'll see model.downshift or model.fallback entries with timestamps. occasionally the field can be null in exported CSVs because of masking, so watch for that in API exports.

[11:20] Kevin Ortiz: security question — what parts of this telemetry leave the VPC in a Private deployment? we need to know data residency and audit logs.

[11:27] Sophie Martinez: for Private customers, the telemetry can be kept in your VPC and the control plane can be configured to not ingest payloads. for hosted API we retain request metadata but payload redaction is available. i'll attach the SOC2 and the Private deployment encryption notes after the call.

[12:15] Tom Reynolds: can we map our correlation id to Redwood's request id? that's key for our logs.

[12:21] Liam Chen: absolutely. we have a header x-rw-correlation-id you can set and it will appear as request.client_id in the console. if you don't set it, we generate rw_request_id.

[13:05] [ambient typing] Liam Chen: demoing a sample where a request hit an upstream webhook and timed out — you'll see a gap in the timeline where the external call waited then an error step was recorded. the error node contains stderr-ish text, stack snippets, and the server response code. sometimes the auto-transcription breaks up long error messages.

[15:00] Aisha Patel: our upstream webhooks sometimes return 502 for 30s under load then come back; will the console help separate transient 502 spikes vs systemic regressions?

[15:08] Liam Chen: yes — we have a heatmap of error types over time and the request inspector links horizontally to a cohort view. you can group by error code and then drill into failed-request timelines. we also show a rolling percent — to find regressions you can pin a baseline window.

[17:26] Sophie Martinez: quick pause — one thing we recommend is instrumenting two correlation points: a client-side id and a server routing tag. that makes join queries easier when you stitch SIEM logs.

[18:40] Tom Reynolds: you mentioned KV cache metrics earlier, what about visibility into cache size, evictions per minute, and hotkeys?

[18:46] Liam Chen: in the Optimize tab we show cache hit ratio, hot key table, estimated mem usage per model, and eviction rate. hot keys are shown as hashed tokens by default to avoid PII leakage, but you can request raw token logs under a compliance agreement.

[20:05] Marta Kline: is there any smart suggestion auto-surfacing? like 'we saw your hit rate drop when sequence length > 1024, consider quantizing'.

[20:12] Liam Chen: yes that's part of Redwood Optimize suggestions. the console will give flagged recommendations: batching tweaks, model quantization, route pinning. suggestions are heuristic-driven and link to docs. sometimes the wording in the UI is terse — we appended expanded tooltips in the latest patch.

[22:40] [noise: brief static on call] Aisha Patel: can you show the CSV export? we want to pipe it into our Splunk.

[22:48] Liam Chen: sure. export -> request-level -> include fields: rw_request_id, client_id, model, seq_len, kv_cache_hit, compute_ms, external_ms, error_code. export generates a zipped CSV and an S3 presign link. note: packaging sometimes names the column "K V cache" in legacy runs.

[24:10] Tom Reynolds: about replays — would a replay expose secrets? we are paranoid about tokens in prompts.

[24:18] Sophie Martinez: great question. playback redacts model inputs by default; for private pilots we can enable a redaction schema for PII. we also support a tokenization-only replay that shows structural tokenization without content.

[26:00] Marta Kline: show us an example of an error we commonly saw — the long tail where compute jumps after a particular system call.

[26:08] Liam Chen: pulling up one...here you can see a small spike in compute when kernel selection switched to a different matmul path at runtime. that often happens when the serving runtime switches execution kernels due to sequence length. in the console we annotate kernel changes as runtime.labels.kernel_switch.

[28:40] Aisha Patel: is there an alerting hook for kernel_switch? we'd like to be notified when that happens more than X times in an hour because that usually precedes a regression.

[28:48] Liam Chen: yep, you can create a rule in the Alerts tab: event == runtime.labels.kernel_switch AND count > 10 in 60m. alerts can go to Slack, PagerDuty, or a webhook.

[30:10] Tom Reynolds: earlier you said fallback to smaller models could be silent. can we make fallbacks visible in the main ops dashboard?

[30:18] Sophie Martinez: we can add a gate to make fallback events surface as prominent incidents rather than background telemetry; that is a configuration toggle for enterprise customers.

[32:05] Kevin Ortiz: on encryption — where are the telemetry logs stored for Hosted vs Private? and who has access?

[32:12] Sophie Martinez: Hosted: telemetry is stored encrypted at rest in our managed store, access controlled via RBAC and audit logs. Private: telemetry can remain in your VPC storage, we can integrate with your KMS/HSM for encryption. i'll include the architecture diagram in the follow-up.

[34:00] [pause] Liam Chen: quick note on perf testing — when we ran RiverMark-like workload in our test harness we saw batching wins up to 2.2x when sequence length distribution was small and bursty. but when sequence lengths vary widely batching can hurt tail latency. that's why the console provides per-route sequence histograms.

[36:30] Marta Kline: could you run a short pilot where we route a subset of production traffic through Redwood Dedicated for 48 hours? we want to reproduce the incident with real load.

[36:40] Sophie Martinez: yes that's typical — we can stand up a dedicated lane and do a canary at 5-10% traffic. that'll require a small committed window and a security handshake.

[38:10] Aisha Patel: onboarding friction question: how much agent-side instrumentation is needed? our app is in-house Go services.

[38:18] Liam Chen: minimal. you add a request header correlation id and optionally our agent for richer client-side breadcrumbs. for Go, we have a small SDK snippet and a sample middleware — i'll drop the sample repo link.

[40:00] Tom Reynolds: are there size/throughput limits for the console? we process tens of thousands of requests per minute.

[40:06] Sophie Martinez: for Hosted, we sample aggressively for extremely high throughput tiers; Dedicated gives you full ingest with quota. Private can be configured to your retention SLA. we'll share ingestion sizing guidance.

[42:20] Liam Chen: demoing a cascading failure view: you can group requests by upstream dependency and then the console shows a tree of calls, percent failed, median time. it's helpful to quickly find which dependency is the main pain.

[44:00] Marta Kline: do you keep historical per-route models of normal latency so that anomaly detection isn't just rule-based?

[44:06] Liam Chen: yes we have baseline models for each route and we surface anomaly scores. again, you can tune sensitivity. sometimes you'll see false positives on cold-start days.

[45:30] Aisha Patel: ok action recap?

[45:33] Sophie Martinez: recap: 1) Sophie will send SOC2 summary + Private deploy encryption docs + recording; 2) Liam will run KV miss simulation and 48-hour sample bench; 3) RiverMark will send anonymized trace sample and an incident timeline from June 17; 4) we'll propose a 5% canary plan for Dedicated pilot.

[46:05] Tom Reynolds: sounds good. one more quick ask: can you add a custom column in CSV exports for our internal 'txn_id'?

[46:12] Liam Chen: yes we support custom columns from request headers, just add header map.txn_id to the export fields.

[47:00] [wrap-up] Sophie Martinez: thanks all — we'll follow up in email, and we can schedule the pilot planning call next week.
[47:10] Kevin Ortiz: thanks everyone, appreciate it.
[47:15] Marta Kline: thanks.
[47:20] Aisha Patel: thanks, bye.

[54:10] (call ended)
